case_name: Robbins et al. v. Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board
text:
Robbins et al. v. Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board

[1964] 1 O.R. 653-654

ONTARIO

[COURT OF APPEAL]

AYLESWORTH, GIBSON and MacKAY, JJ.A.

10th FEBRUARY 1964.

Administrative law -- Boards and tribunals -- Delegation of power by Farm Products Marketing Board to Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board to make regulations respecting refusal of licences to produce tobacco and refusal and reduction of quotas -- Specific application of legislation to current crop year -- Retrospective effect clear -- Plan in skeleton form satisfying requirements of Act.

The judgment of the Court was delivered orally by

[Reference re Farm Products Marketing Act, 1957 CanLII 1 (SCC), 7 D.L.R. (2d) 257, [1957] S.C.R. 198, folld]

APPEALS from a judgment and order of Grant, J., ante, p. 56, 1963 CanLII 283 (ON HCJ), 41 D.L.R. (2d) 107, dismissing an action against defendant Board and an application against it for mandamus.

C.L. Dubin, Q.C., and M.M. Green, for appellants.

H.E. Harris, Q.C., and L.S. Geiger, for respondent.

AYLESWORTH, J.A.:-- These are appeals argued together from a judgment and order of Grant, J. [1963 CanLII 283 (ON HCJ), 41 D.L.R. (2d) 107, [1964] 1 O.R. 56], pronounced on October 9th last, wherein he dismissed an action brought by Robbins et al. against the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board and an application for mandamus brought by Atkins et al. against the same board.

In the observations the Court has to make the defendant, respondent, that is the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board, will be referred to as the local Board and the Farm Products Marketing Board will be referred to as the Board. The issues here are with respect to 1963 crops of tobacco.

We are in agreement with the reasons of as well as the result arrived at by Grant, J., and it will suffice to express our further views as follows: Reading the statute as a whole and the somewhat unusually broad powers of delegation therein conferred upon the Board we think the regulations of the Board and of the local Board are quite within their respective powers and in conformity with the Act. Moreover, the refusal to allot acreage and/or to fix marketing quotas does not require, in our view, a specific regulation where a licence has been refused and we think a licence for the 1963 crop was required as will be made to appear later. In our view such a regulation would be superfluous with respect to the applicants who have been refused a licence. We think that it is clearly manifested, and on this again we agree with Grant, J., in the 1963 legislation that that legislation is intended by the very wording thereof to apply to the 1963 crop and, of course, the regulations enacted by the Board and the local Board clearly in their terms purport to apply to the 1963 crop. In that sense the legislation with sufficient clarity, in our view, is retrospective in effect with respect to matters concerning the 1963 crop but we think the matter does not rest there. Section 18 [of the Farm Products Marketing Act, R.S.O. 1960, c. 137], the whole of which was enacted in 1963 [1962-63, c. 45, s. 11], has a definition of "producing" therein appearing in s-s. (1), cl. (b) and we think "planting" as mentioned in the definition of producing means the planting of the tobacco plants in the fields and does not include the propagation of the seeds in the greenhouses preliminary to such planting.

Mr. Dubin also takes the point that the plan or purported plan is in fact and in law no such plan as is contemplated and required by the statute. The plan, skeleton in form though it may be, in our view, is a plan as contemplated by the Act and we are supported in that conclusion by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, appearing in 1957 CanLII 1 (SCC), 7 D.L.R. (2d) 257, [1957] S.C.R. 198 in the case of Reference re the Farm Products Marketing Act.

In the result the appeals are dismissed with costs. In taxing the costs of the appeals, since the matters were argued together, the taxing officer will take that into consideration and allow one counsel fee, that is to say that whatever counsel fee or fees are allowed will be spread over the two matters and there will not be a counsel fee or fees separately allowed with respect to each appeal.

Appeals dismissed.
